No man working in the interest of the country would build such a wharf in a place like that when there are dozens of locations, half a mile or more further down, where the wharf could be properly built, and where it could do some good. The tide there runs, I think, from twenty-three to twenty-seven feet. These are the conditions, and they must be faced. Laying aside the question of the location of the wharf-a location which, as I have said, no engineer would choose if he wanted to make this wharf a public utility to Canada-there are special conditions to be considered. In the first place, in making a foundation for a concrete wharf you must allow for the twenty-seven foot rise and fall of the tide. Then, you must have at least ten feet above high water to allow a vessel to lie alongside the wharf. Then, below the lowest level of the water, you must have whatever depth you wish to allow for a vessel to come to the wharf. If you allow for vessels of twenty-foot draught, you must allow altogether fifty-seven feet from the top of the wharf to the river bottom. They did not dredge the foundations of the wharf far enough, and so when they tried to get the twenty feet or whatever it was they wanted, the whole thing spilled out into the river. I hope the minister will explain some of the things I have described. If my description is not in accordance with the facts, I want him to say so. He must have the information on this subject. He must know how much water there is in front of the wharf; how much there is on the upper side and how much on the lower side. He must know the width of the cracks in the concrete slabs. He must know the variation of level of this wharf and how much filling they were afraid to put in the centre and so filled in with piling covered with planks.
Since my visit to that wharf I have received more than a dozen letters on the subject. Unfortunately most of them are anonymous, and so I do not wish to lay them before the House. But if I should read them I think the minister would be somewhat surprised to learn what some of his constituents think of this work. I have here one.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: Is it anonymous?

Yes. The writer says:
I will give you my name when living under a better administration, but circumstances force me to conceal my identity.
I will send this letter to the minister if he likes.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
Never mind. I think
neither of us takes much stock in anonymous letters.	*

It comes from some one who dared not reveal his identity. I tell you, Mr. Chairman, this work is a shame and a disgrace to Canada; it is something which the Minister of Marine and Fisheries cannot laugh away, something he cannot get rid of with a jocular remark. It is a matter which the people of St. John expect him to face. It is so disgraceful that it will require something more than a laugh and a joke on his part to set it right.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: My hon. friend from Carle-ton (Mr. Carvell) is never extremely moderate in his language, and in his speech of to-day he has not departed from his usual style. Permit me to say, I had not the slightest thought of dismissing the subject with a laugh or a joke. The marine depot was a necessity at St. John, in consequence of the ballast wharf previously used for the purpose of storing buoys, chains, etc., having been transferred to a company which erected on the site a large sugar refinery. That fact was realized by my hon. friend from the city of St. John (Mr. Pugsley) when he was a member of the Administration. In the Public Works Estimates of 1909-10-I think it was that year-an item appeared of $50,000 as the first instalment toward the construction of a marine depot at St. John. I understand that my hon. friend had in view a site farther up the harbour than this
Over the Reversible Falls.
Oh, that would be all right; it is beyond the current.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: That would be all right, but there would be difficulty in getting up and down the falls.
Vessels could pass twice a day.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
The necessity for the work was recognized by everybody. The Marine Department must have a place for storage, and it must be a wharf in order that the vessels may go and take the articles required to the points where they are to be placed from time to time. So, we looked
for a site. My hon. friend (Mr. Carve'll) speaks of finding a site further down the harbour, but it is most difficult to secure a site on the harbour of St. John for any purpose.
Would not there be a site along by Hilliard's mill?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
I think that that property was one of those offered to us. But the prices were many times in excess of the site where the wharf has been constructed. After full consideration of the matter, this site was purchased, and it was purchased at a price less than the valuation placed upon it by three gentlemen in St. John, all familiar with real estate conditions. One of those was Mr. Fred Sayre, and another was Mr. Lockhart. I. think there was a third, but I have forgotten who it was. The city of St. John made us a gift of their rights in certain lots. The wharf was designed by the engineers of the Marine and Fisheries Department. The chief engineer is Col. Anderson, a man of the highest professional qualifications and standing who has been in the department for over forty years. The assistant engineer is Mr. Basil Fraser who has been assistant engineer, I think, for about twenty years-my hon. friend from Russell (Mr. Murphy) will know. The designs were prepared in the department under the direct instructions of these gentlemen, who, before preparing them, had visited St. John and inspected the site, and so knew exactly what was wanted to meet the needs of the situation. Their reports are in the department. After the designs were completed, tenders were asked for, and the contract was awarded to the lowest tenderer;.
The whaTf has been constructed under the direction of engineers of the Marine and Fisheries Department, who tell me that they are prepared to justify everything that was done in connection with the work. In a tidal harbour difficulties are always encountered in wharf construction; I think this is the first concrete wharf ever built at the city of St. John. I desire to say that there is nothing in connection with this whole matter that is not open to the fullest inquiry and investigation on the part of members of the House. There was a settlement at the front of the wharf which did cause a certain cracking at the front.
It is cracked all along the sides as well.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: No, it is not.
I was there and saw it; in the river side you will find cracks in the concrete.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: It is not cracked all along the side; I have been there, too. My hon. friend speaks of this wharf as if it were a tumble-down structure.
When did the hon. minister see it last?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: About the first of January. If I can rely on my engineers-and I think I can-the wharf is as solid a structure as it can be; the slight settlement that has taken place has in no way impaired its strength. As to my hon. friend's assertion that vessels cannot lie at the front of the wharf without being smashed to pieces, I need only say that the vessels of the Marine Department, the Aberdeen and the Lans-downe, have been docked at the face of the wharf time and again since its construction. The main part of the wharf is all that could be required for the placing upon it of the large buoys which are used' in the Bay of Fundy, and the different things required in connection with the buoy service. When I was there, buoys running up into hundreds of tons in weight were upon that wharf. The storehouses are built further back, in the position recommended by the engineers as the most convenient, having regard to the uses to which the wharf is to be put.
What is the depth of water at the lower side?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: It is not very great; I cannot give the exact figures. At the front it is deep.
How far below the surface of the mud at the lower side of the wharf is the bottom dredged?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: I cannot tell that.

My hon. friend must
realize how important these things are.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
I know that they are important. The engineers of my department say that the wharf was constructed with the view of having it dredged on the lower side. It can be dredged on the lower side to a depth amply sufficient for the boats of the Marine Department. Arrangements have been made with the Public Works Department by which that dredging, if it has not already been done, will be done in the near future. The engineers, who were vested with the control of operations from the time the con-
tract was made, tell me that the wharf is a thoroughly substantial and excellent structure . in every way, that it will admirably serve the purpose for which it was constructed and will last for very many years. Some engineers hold that concrete construction in tidal waters is a mistake. I know an eminent harbour engineer in the province of Quebec who thinks that wharfs in tidal waters should be constructed not of concrete, ' but of timber. However, time will establish whether or not that view is correct. I myself am not an engineer; I rely upon the opinion of those in whom I have confidence; those opinions I have stated to-the Committee. My hon. friend is at liberty to see every file and paper in connection with this transaction from the very first to the very last. My instructions to Colonel Anderson and to Mr. Fraser were to see that the work was carried out thoroughly and well, to give no advantage to anybody for political reasons, and to see that the contract was carried out to the letter and with due regard to the public interest. Had I known that this matter was coming up today in the way that it has, I should have brought with me information as to the depth of dredging, the depth to which the concrete is laid, and so on.

What is the depth of
water at low tide on the face or river side of the wharf?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: It is deep enough for the Aberdeen and the Lansdowne, which are the two boats used by the Marine Department in the buoy service in the Bay of Fundy. I presume it is at least fifteen feet. I will send my hon. friend the information as to this.
Will the hon. minister send me a copy of the plans and specifications of the foundation part? I am not so particular about the concrete.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service

speechtext: That is a very fair offer, but I should prefer having the blue prints.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: If I can get them, I will.
There is plenty of time; any time during the session will do. The wharf will probably stand during the next three or four months.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
Perhaps longer than you
and I will stand.

I should like to have
the information before the session closes. I am not casting any reflection on Colonel Anderson; that is why I want to see the plans. Until I have an opportunity of examining them, I am going to assume that the plans and specifications are all right. I have no doubt that if the wharf had been built according to the plans and specifications, we would not have the condition of affairs that we have to-day. I am objecting not to the plans and specificatioAs, but to the way the work was carried out in St-John. It is a fact that a proper foundation was not made, that the old boulders were not removed from the foundation, and that the filling of the cribwork went down from the very top. You can see great holes inside the concrete slabs where the filling that was put into the cribwork has gone down and out. The holes may be filled up now, but they were there last September. I am glad that my hon. friend takes such an optimistic view of this matter, but I do not agree that a concrete structure which shows cracks from five to seven inches wide, running down perhaps twenty-five or thirty feet, will remain standing for all time.
He has more faith in this crib standing up without any visible means of support than I have or the people of St. John have. Many men to whom I have talked expect to see the thing go to pieces at any time. I make the prophecy that if the Minister of Marine occupies the position he does to-day for two years more, he will either tear the thing down and build it anew or build another wharf around it.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: Will my hon. friend make a little sporting bet on that?	.
Yes, I will make a prophecy anyway.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
I will tell him what I am willing to do with him. If his prophecy proves true, I shall be very glad to give $500 or $1,000, or whatever amount may be agreed upon, to any charity the hon. gentleman may name. If it does not prove
true, I want him to give a similar amount to one I will name. Perhaps this should not go in Hansard.
I will hold the stakes.
I. am afraid my hon. friend might be disposed to let the thing stand up a little longer than would be safe in order to get my thousand dollars.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: It will be there when you and I have shuffled off this mortal coil.
He is gambling on a sure thing, because he will not be there.

My hon. friend can not get away from this condition of affairs by any such sporting offer as this. He has to face the situation as it is, and if I have improperly described it, he is at liberty to describe it properly and to set me right where I am wrong. But I have not improperly described it; I have described it as it is. I have not painted the picture as black as it is; and before the session of Parliament is over, we will be able to show other works in St. John of very much greater importance than this that are just as bad as this, and show exactly the same condition of political corruption existing in other portions of the harbour of St. John as I am afraid existed in this portion.

The Minister of Marine states that my hon. friend from Carleton, N.B. (Mr. Carvell), ie not usually moderate in his expressions of opinion and has not been so in this ease. I have observed thlalt the hon. member for Oaitetom, N.B., does not very often go wrong. He has a faculty for finding out where errors have been committed and where wrong has been done, and perhaps, when he has discovered those errors and those instances of wrong-doing he is pretty forceful in the expression of his opinion. I do not think any one could blame him for that, that is his duty. He is here, a member of Parliament, representing a portion of the people of this country, and I think in this matter, as in other matters which he has felt it his duty do bring to the attention of Parliament and of the country, he has simply been doing what was absolutely correct and should be expected of him as a member of this House. The hon. member has made a very strong; statement, which has not been answered by the minister. He has stated that upon the southern side of this wharf there is scarcely any water, and that if the mud there is dredged out

to a depth sufficient to allow vessels to lie there at low tide, the structure will tumble over to the south and become a wreck.
' Mr. HAZEN: The engineer of the department says very differently.

My hon. friend the
minister says he went there in January of this year, and yet he cannot tell the depth of the water on the southern side of the wharf which he has constructed in his own constituency, in his home city, and in which he has evidently taken a pride. He cannot say whether the depth of water is one foot or five feet.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: It has always been intended to dredge that out.

But does not my hon.
friend see, as a gentleman having ordinary judgment, that you cannot dredge out on the southern side of the wharf unless the wharf setting runs down to at least one or two feet lower than you are going to dredge?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: Exactly, and the engineers say that is being done, that it is to be dredged out sufficiently for boats to lie there at low tide.

The hon. member for
Carleton says that the foundation has evidently not been properly prepared for the wharf. He has also stated that there is a great crack, in fact, not only one crack, but several, extending from the top of the wharf right down to the lowest part, and that it can be seen at low tide.
And that is on the lower side of the wharf as well as on the face and to some extent on the upper side, but not to the same extent as on the lower side and on the face.

That is an extremely
serious statement, and yet my hon. friend the minister, who was there only -a few weeks ago, does not deny it.,

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
I do deny the statement
that the wharf was all cracked.

Of course, the hon.
member for Carleton does not mean that there are not some parts of it that have no cracks, because if it was all cracks there would be no wharf: it would be all space and no solidity. When my hon. friend from Carleton states that there are large cracks extending from the top to low water, both in the front and lower side, and on the upper side as well

To some extent on the
upper side as well.
That is right.
Mr. Boone is not a wharf builder.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: The Boones are a family oi wharf builders; his father was one before him.
Mr. Boone of St. Mary's?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: Yes, the Boones and the Haines have been building wharves for years.

Mr. Boone may have built some small wharves on the river St. John, costing from ?500 to $1,000, but he is not a wharf builder in the sense of being a contractor for large wharves in tidal waters. I venture to say that he never built a concrete wharf in his life. Is the minister able to say that Mr. Boone has 'had experience in concrete work?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: I think he had in connection with piers and bridges; I am so informed.

At all events, Mr. Boone has not been a wharf builder in the sense of building wharves in tidal waters, and the rumour is that he was not the real contractor, but that the parties really interested in the contract were political friends of the minister, residing in the city of St. John.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: I know that Mr. Boone was there on the work from first to last, from morning till night, while the work was under construction.
Then can the minister tell us what experience Mr. Mosher had?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: He is a practical man; I know he has had practical experience.
Where does he reside?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: At St. Martin's.
What is his business?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: He is a lumberman.
When I was Minister of Public Works I was always very careful to see that in works of this character we had as local inspector a man of a great deal of experience.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: In addition to Mr. Mosher, the engineer of the department was there every day.
But Mr. Mosher was supposed to be the inspector.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: Subject to the orders oi the engineer of the department.
Mr. Mosher has had no experience in concrete work, and yet he is the man upon whom the engineer would depend.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: He is a very practical man.
He may be a very practical man, but unless he understands work of this character, the work is apt to suffer. Then I would like to know what experience Mr. Macdonald has had of concrete work.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: He is a competent engineer, and I presume he has had experience in building.

It is important for us to know what experience Mr. Macdonald has had in this class of work, because there is the lamentable fact, if what the hon. member for Carleton states is true- and I have not the slightest doubt that what he states from his own observation is true-a very deplorable piece of work has been perpetrated in connection with this contract. I would suggest to the minister that we had better have the matter cleared up before the item passes, and that he produce all the papers in connection with the work. Then the matter can be threshed out, and if there is no fault to be found I shall be very glad. I am sure that no one will be better pleased to find that there was no fault than my honourable friend from Carleton. It gives me, and I am sure, it gives him, no pleasure to find fault; we would rather be in the position of being able to praise work that has been done. I would like to see the works at St. John of so substantial a character that they would be a credit to the Government and a source of pride to the community. It will not lead to any delay to let this item stand, and to have



the papers and reports in connection with the wharf at St. John brought down.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: I do not think that anything is gained by allowing an item to stand. I want the House to get the fullest information, and I am perfectly prepared, when the motion is made, to bring down all the papers, correspondence, and contracts in connection with this matter. Rather than put my honourable friend to the trouble of moving for a return I am even prepared to give him the information without any formality at all. If there is to be an investigation based on those papers, surely the place to pursue it would be the Public Accounts Committee, where there would be an opportunity of calling witnesses connected with the work. I have no desire to avoid the fullest investigation into this matter, but I would suggest that the item be passed, and I will consider the motion far a return made and bring down the papers. Of course the purpose of the inquiry would be shown in the motion, and perhaps it would be better if such a motion were made. I would be very glad indeed to ask Colonel Anderson and my deputy minister to place everything before my hon. friends if they care to come to the department. I do not like to delay the passage of Estimates if it can be avoided.

I think the minister will see that, while we appreciate his offer, to go to the department would place us at a great disadvantage. I have not sufficient knowledge of enginering to digest plans and specifications and other papers in connection with a work of this kind in an .hour and a half or an hour, which would be as long as an officer in Colonel Anderson's position could afford to spend with us. But if I had those documents I think I would be able to fairly digest them, and I think my hon. friend from St. John would have the same ability. I am not particular as to whether the item passes or not. I think it would be better to let it stand, because after an investigation of these plans and papers I would like to make some other remarks. I look upon it as a matter of such grave importance that we should have a chance of discussing it with a full knowledge of the facts.	.
Item allowed to stand.

The minister has given
us the items for New Brunswick, but not for the province of Quebec.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: In Quebec the1 works contemplated are at Amherst Island, one' of the Magdalens, a new lighthouse and fog alarm costing $25,000; at the Upper Traverse, repairs to pier, $8,000; buoys and beacons, $10,000; general improvements, $15,000; unforeseen works and repairs, $25,000; Quebec agency, repairs to wharf, $22,000; in all $100,000.

Is $25,000 not a large sum to expend on a lighthouse?
Mr/ HAZEN: It is for a lighthouse and fog alarm. The light is to be a very powerful one, and there is also to be a powerful alarm.
Lighthouse and coast service-signal service,
560,000.
What is the nature of that service? Is it in connection with wireless telegraphy?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: Signal stations have been established for years for the purpose of maintaining communication between shipping and the shore. These are located at St. John, Halifax, Cape Race, and on the river St. Lawrence, and the Great Lakes as far west as Sault Ste. Marie.

How much is expended
on the service?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: The vote is $60,000. In 1914-15, out of our total vote of $60,000, we spent $52,310, and up to the 31st December we spent $42,516.
Is there a Marconi station on the Baie des Chaleurs?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: No, I do not think so. There are stations at Fame Point, Quebec, St. John, and Halifax.
Has the minister considered the advisability of having a lifesaving station on the Baie des Chaleurs?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: I do not think that the technical officers of the department consider it necessary, because they say that a ship in the Baie des Chaleurs could communicate by wireless with either Quebec or Fame Point.
The great bulk of the steamers going up the Baie des Chaleurs are not equipped with wireless.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: All ships under the law, if they are on a voyage that takes them a certain distance from land, have to be equipped with wireless.
Whether they carry, passengers or not?'

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: Yes; but, of course, vessels on the Baie des Chaleurs are always in sight of land, and they would not come under that provision.
Lumber boats are not equipped with wireless.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: No.

Yet they go across the ocean.
The committee took recess.

speakerposition: subtopic

speechtext:
My hon. friend from South Renfrew (Mr. Graham) referred the other day with appreciation to the work that had been performed by the Pubic Works Department in equipping this building so promptly and conveniently for the purposes of Parliament. If I may be permitted, I would like to express my warm appreciation of the indefatigable energy and personal .attention which my hon. friend the Minister of Public Works (Mr. Rogers) himself has given, to these matters. I have personal knowledge that he has been most laiotive and indefatigable, ever since we met here on Friday afternoon last, and certainly the arrangements which have been thus carried out have been much more satisfactory than could have been expected., He desired me to announce to the committee tkat the time-honoured custom of having the lightabovethe Parliament buildings will be carried out in the future.
