speakerposition: topic
stagedirection
speechtext:
The House in Committee of Supply, Mr. Rhodes in the Cnair.
Lighthouse and coast service-administration of pilotage and maintenance and repairs, to steamer Eureka, $56,300.
What steamer is that?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
The pilot steamer at Father Point on which the pilots go to and come from vessels, and which has been in the service for a number of years. This is the same appropriation as we had last year. In 1914-15, we spent $42,904.64, and the expenditure up to the 31st of December, 1915, was $33,026.10. The expenditure next year . will, we expect, be considerably under the estimate, hut we think it wise to ask for the same amount as we asked for before,, because it may be found necessary to makes some extensive repairs upon the boat.
Lighthouse and coast service-maintenance and repairs to wharves, $10,000.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: We receive this vote every year. As hon. gentlemen know, after wharves are constructed by the Department of Public Works they automatically come under the management of the Department of Marine and Fisheries, and when repairs are necessary, our department puts repairs on the wharves to an amount not exceeding $50 in each case. If larger amounts are required, they have to be put in the Estimates of the Department of Public Works. In 1914-15 we spent $9,993 and, up to the 31st of December, 1915, we spent ..$4,731.13.

Where are these wharves
situated?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
Everywhere throughout
Canada on the coasts and lakes.

Do I understand that when repairs amount to more than $50, the work is done by the Department of Public
Works?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: Yes.

I call the attention of the minister to a wharf at Margaree-harbour that was constructed some seven or eight years ago at a cost of four or five or six thousand dollars. That whaTf has been in a disabled condition for the last, four years, and can not be used at all. It will take $25 to repair it.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: At present?
Yes, at present, and for the last three years. It is absolutely useless now, for the simple reason that no attention has been paid to it.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: We will have it repaired right away.
I made an effort before to get it repaired, but unfortunately 1 am' on this side of the House.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: I shall be very glad to have it repaired. That is a thing to be attended to promptly.
Are the large harbours under the department of my hon. friend?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: Some of them.

I do not know why it should be so, but it has always been the case that these harbours are under different heads. For instance, the Toronto harbour is under the Harbour Commission at the present time. Does it come under the Department of Marine and Fisheries?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: Yes.
And still a good deal of work is being done by the Public Works Department.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: Nearly all of it.
I suppose my hon. friend would not be in a position to tell me how the work is going on because he is not doing it.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
No, the Public Works
Department.

How much has the
Marine Department spent on the harbour at Toronto?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
I do not think we have
spent a dollar in that harbour on wharves, dredging, or work of that sort. There is a life-saving station in the harbour, which comes under the control of the Department of the Naval Service, but I suppose it is not to things of that kind that the hon. gentleman refers.

I took some little part
when the present Harbour Commission for Toronto was established, and I would like to find out how it is progressing. In years gone by, I think, Toronto had the poorest harbour facilities of any of our great cities in the way of loading and unloading, and when the Commission was formed great improvement was expected. But that imfMr. A. W. Chisholm. 1
provement, I think, has not arrived with the rapidity that was looked for. I do not know whether there has been friction be tween the Government appointees and the city appointees, or whether they are getting along harmoniously-

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
There are commissions
and commissions. The Montreal Harbour Commissioners, for instance, are all appointed by the Government of Canada. It might be said that they are, in a sense, a branch of the Marine and Fisheries Department. The title of the harbour is vested in these Commissioners. They prepare their plans for improvements, and get the approval of the Governor General in Council on the recommendation of the Marine and Fisheries Department for what they undertake to do. Then, under authority that is given us by Parliament, by Acts passed from time to time, we advance them money for the work. The work is carried on and is inspected by the officer in charge. The Harbour Commissioners pay the interest on the money that we have advanced. So, it may be said that improvements there cost Canada nothing, because interest is paid on all the money advanced. Of course, it cost Canada something in this way,-the interest they pay is three and a half per cent which was about the rate the Dominion paid at the time the Act was passed, but, of course, money costs the country more now. The organization of the Harbour Commission of Toronto is different from that of the Montreal Commission.	Some of
the members are appointed by the Governor in Council, some by the city council and some, I think, by the Board of Trade. They do not borrow money from us, but they administer the harbour, collect the harbour, dues, such as they are, and carry out improvements. They do not act directly under the control of the Marine and Fisheries Department. Then, there are some harbours that are not managed by a commission. For instance, there is the harbour of St. John. The City Council is the conservator of the harbour and appoints a harbour master. The Government has built public works there which have come under the control of the Department of Marine and Fisheries. The department appoints wharfingers who collect dues, and the money, which amounts to a considerable sum each year, goes into the Consolidated Revenue Fund. The hon. gentleman will thus see that there are dif-

ferent organizations governing different harbours.
Will the hon. gentleman give me the names of the Toronto Harbour Commissioners?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
I thought that would be
found in the report of the department, but while I find here the report of the harbour master, I do not see the names of the commissioners.

Referring to the Auditor General's report of expenditure under the heading " Repairs to Wharves," I find last year a large part of the money was spent in watching sheds. I find the names of sixteen men paid $2 or $2.50 a day, from January to April, for watching sheds. Will the minister please explain?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: It was necessary last year, as a precautionary measure, to put guards on our sheds and wharves.
Were all these men on the same wharf?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: I should not think so. We have two wharves in the city of St. John used by the large ships in the winter season. The sheds on these wharves have to be guarded both night and day in case of an attempt being made to destroy them. Any successful attempt of that kind would hamper the trade of the country tremendously, and would also interfere with the transport of munitions and other articles going forward for use in the war.

Have the resident
engineers of the Department of Marine and Fisheries instructions to report the small repairs to wharves that may be needed? If not, in what way does the department receive information on this subject?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: The resident engineers are expected to report to the engineers' branch of the department in Ottawa any need of small repairs that may arise, and they do so, so far as I know.

To the Engineers'
Branch of the Public Works or of the Marine and Fisheries?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: Small repairs are reported to the Marine and Fisheries. But if the amount involved is over, say, $50, it would be the duty of the resident engineers of the Public Works Department to report to the department to which they belong.
I have an idea that a great many resident engineers understand it to be their duty to report only to the Public Worktp. Department, '

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: They are quite right. 1 think perhaps the hon. gentleman misunderstood me. It is the duty of the resident engineers of the Marine Department to report where small repairs are necessary, but in the case of larger repairs, the engineer, of the Department of Publie Works reports to the department to which he belongs.
And then is it the duty of the Department of Public Works to communicate with the Department of Marine and Fisheries?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: No.	.

I know many cases in which th'e resident engineers have had their attention called to the need of repairs to wharves built for the accommodation of fishermen, and in nearly every case the engineer of the Department of Publie Works was ignorant of the fact that provision had been made whereby money could be obtained from the Department of Marine and Fisheries to make these repairs. Instructions should be sent to resident engineers that this money is available, so that they can act on ^ the principle C(A stitch in time saves nine.

I understand that the Montreal Harbour Commissioners were appointed by the Governor in Council on the recommendation of the Minister of Marine and Fisheries.. As the minister has explained, the. Government provides the money and the Harbour Commissioners pay the interest on that money at the rate of 3J per cent, the title of the harbour property being vested in the commissioners.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: That was the case until the last session of Parliament. In order to obviate the difficulty arising from a proposed civic taxation of wharves, which would run into millions of dollars, we passed an Act at the last session, approved by the Montreal city council, declaring that this harbour property was the property of the Crown.

I think it was the late Sir William Van Horne, who, discussing the question of transportation, endeavoured to emphasize the importance of keeping the harbour of Montreal in an efficient state in order to cope with, the inward and outward traffic that ought to pass through that

port annually. During the season of navigation Montreal is the centre of a great traffic, both inward and outward. No matter how efficient are the transportation facilities afforded between Eastern and Western Canada, unless the outlet and inlet be properly equipped the handling of the traffic will be greatly handicapped and cannot reach its highest state of efficiency. We have expended many millions of dollars in the construction of canals; at the present time we are really building a.new.Welland canal. Many millions have been expended on harbours west of Montreal, in the Great Lakes and along the river St. Lawrence, and large sums have been expended in the system of canals from Cardinal east. With the three transcontinental railways, the harbours of Quebec and Montreal, as well as those of the Maritime provinces, must be kept in an efficient state, otherwise the expenditure of money for navigation purposes and railway facilities between Eastern and Western Canada will avail nothing. It is the object of Canadians, I believe, not only to carry our own traffic east and west, but so to improve our facilities that we shall be able to carry a portion of the traffic of the great nation to the south. I have never had any fear, no matteT what tariff policy might be adopted, that Canadian transportation facilities -would not be kept busy by the traffic that would come to them. During the past year Montreal has handled a great deal of grain. An enormous crop of grain has been taken from the West, and 1 think it is in contemplation to increase still further the facilities at Montreal harbour. The Harbour Commissioners of Montreal, |an able body of men, as they always have been, find themselves very much crowded at this time by the movement of our western crop. I think the ratepayers of Canada are all interested in the question of how to get the products of the farm carried to the factory with rapidity and at a reasonable rate. These harbours, which afford an inlet and outlet for the great traffic of Canada, must be looked after to the utmost of our financial ability, because by equipping them adequately we provide the means of increasing the value of our products. Can the minister tell us what are the proposed improvements of the facilities in Montreal,
1 what improvements have been made this season, and what is the plain of the Harbour Commissioners for the future? With the further development of the West, and with the continued large production in our
IMr. Graham.]
eastern provinces, the necessity for the development of Montreal harbour becomes more pressing. I have been reading during the past few, days of the increased traffic through Montreal which is destined for ports in the Hnited States. We want to afford such facilities that it will be cheaper and more expeditious not only for ourselves but for at least a portion of the United States as well to send their traffic through our ports, giving our ships, railways and workingmen the advantage of handling that traffic, and at the same time giving our own producers and consumers the benefit that must come from the improvement of our transportation facilities.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
My hon. friend is quite right in the statements that he makes. A few years ago the port of Montreal was a very small port from the standpoint of grain shipments; to-day it is the largest grain port in America. The total quantity of grain received at or transferred in the harbour in 1906 was only 944,321 bushels. In 1908 it was 8,661,000 bushels; in 1911, 21,007,000,; in 1912, 25,000,000; in 1913, 43,349,000; in 1914, 62,318,000. So, from 1912 to 1914 there was the enormous increase of 37,000,000 bushels. The harbour facilities have been pronounced by port authorities who have inspected them to be among the very best on the continent of North America. Only two years ago. the port authorities of New York published a report approving in the highest terms of the work of the Harbour Commissioners of Montreal and the method on which their work was being carried out. As my hon. friend has intimated, the commissioners have done excellent work. The commission that was in charge of the work when I came to office, consisting of Mr. Stephens, Mr. Ballantyne and Mr. Geoffrion, was an excellent commission, and I deeply regretted that these gentlemen, after serving for some time, felt that owing to the pressure of private business it was necessary for them to hand in their resignation. Mr. Ballantyne had told me some time before that -it would be impossible for him to continue, owing to the necessity for his giving attention to large private interests. Being impressed with the value of his work, I urged him to continue it, but after considering the matter he decided that he could not do - so, expressing his deep regret, and bis appreciation, of my urging him to stay. I am glad to say that I was able to make recommendation to council, after consulting the Board of Trade

and business interests in Montreal, for the appointment of three gentlemen who have proved to be worthy successors of the members of the former commission. The work of the present commission, consisting of Mr. W. J. Ross, Mr. Farquhar Robertson, and General Labelle, has been progressive and prudent, and has, I think, met the views of those interested in the trade and traffic of Montreal. They have been adding to their elevator accommodation and are contemplating further additions during the present year. My hon. friend will find in the last report of the Department of Marine and Fisheries an extract from the report of the Montreal Harbour Commissioner regarding the further storage that is required. From that extract and from my personal conversations with the. commissioners, I think I may say that they are improving the elevator accommodation there as rapidly as is feasible, to meet the existing conditions and requirements. They are making also arrangements for further extensive warehouses and sheds made necessary on account of increasing business; and so long as Canada grows, so long as Canadian trade grows, so long will Montreal grow and so long will further facilities have to be prepared, year after year, if that port, the great entrepot of Canada in the summer, is to keep pace with the growing importance and,trade of the country.

Has there not been a
considerable falling off in the trade of the harbour of Montreal during 1915?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
The revenues last year
showed a decrease. That was in consequence of war conditions and the difficulty of getting tonnage.

Could the minister give
an idea of the quantity of Canadian grain that went by American ports?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
Of course, a very large
quantity goes ,by American ports every year; but, on the other hand, during the year ended 31st March, 1915, a very considerable quantity of American grain went out of Montreal.

Is there any hope that
during this season Montreal will be better supplied with tonnage than last year?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
I am in .hopes that as this grain is necessary to feed the people on the other side of the water the British Admiralty will see the necessity of providing plenty of transports for carrying the grain,
as they are now doing for freight from Maritime Province ports.
Will the steamers now running to Halifax and St. John run to Montreal in summer?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: I have no doubt they will, as many of the war supplies now passing through Maritime ports will be sent through St. Lawrence ports in summer. I have no doubt the Admiralty will arrange to have similar transports plying to St. Lawrence ports during summer.

Could the minister say
anything in regard to the harbour of Quebec, in view of the opening and operation of the Transcontinental railway?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
The report of the Harbour Commissioners of Quebec is to be found in the last report of the Department of Marine and Fisheries, at page 309. The work has proceeded very satisfactorily, and the facilities afforded in the harbour for the accommodation of large vessels are better than ever before. I quote this paragraph from the report of the commissioners, the report [DOT]of their very efficient engineer, Mr. Boswell:
The facilities offered in the harbour of Quebec for the accommodation of large vessels have been demonstrated in a decisive manner when the embarkation of the first Canadian overseas contingent took place in the latter part of September. Thirty-one steamships, [DOT] ranging in tonnage from 4,686 tons to 18,564 tons have been accommodated at the commis1-sioners' deep-water docks and wharves for taking on board the men, horses, ammunition and supplies of the first contingent. Several of these vessels were bunkered here, and sup-* plied with fresh water from the commissioners' water works, which are connected with the city water works.
Work has been done at the Louise embankment, and elevator accommodation at Quebec is completed and ready to handle grain. The new elevator is of the most modern type and thoroughly efficient.
Is it being utilized this winter?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: It is in a condition to be utilized. I do not know whether there is any grain there or not, but, of course, it will not be until navigation of the St. Lawrence commences that it will be actively used. I certainly hope that Quebec will become a great grain port, and that grain coming over the National Transcontinental railway will go to Quebec, so that the facilities that have been provided will prove a great blessing to the port and a great business convenience.
The very extensive improvements in the harbour are being done by the Public Works Department?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: Improvements in Quebec harbour have been carried out by several departments. The harbour commissioners have done very extensive work there. The extension of the embankment around towards the river St. Charles, which will afford accommodation for some of the largest class of ocean steamships, is being done by them. They have also erected an elevator at that point. Then the Public Works Department have been doing certain very important work, and are now engaged in important work at the St. Charles river, designed to furnish a harbour for the smaller trading vessels.

I understand that the improvements on the public wharfs of the country are under the control of the Department of Marine and Fisheries up to $50. Take the province of New Brunswick. I think the department has only one resident engineer at St. John. Under these conditions, who reports to the department on the condition of the smaller wharfs throughout the province?
Mr- HAZEN: The wharfinger. He occupies a small position and is paid by a percentage on his collections. He is appointed by an Qrder in Council. The wharfinger is supposed to report either to the agent of the department in the province, or, if he thinks fit, to the department direct. It may be that wharfingers sometimes fail to do so; their remuneration is small, and there may be occasions when they neglect to report. But clearly it is the wharfinger's business. He should report either to the agent of the department at St. John, who would communicate with us, or to the resident engineer at St. John who would report to the department.

The reason I asked the
question is that I had occasion during last summer to go round different places in the province, and I noticed that there were a number of small wharfs which could be repaired at very little cost for the accommodation and convenience of those who use them, but which, if not repaired, would in time involve a considerable expenditure. This is particularly so in the case of the small wharfs on the rivers. When the ice goes out in the spring it is apt to damage these small wharfs, and unless the repairs are attended to at once, a greater expenditure is rendered necessary.
TMr. Hazen.]
I would suggest that there should be some official of the department in each county whose business it would be to report to the department when repairs to these small wharfs are necessary. It would be a great saving to the department, and a great convenience to those who use the wharfs.
Lighthouse and coast service-to provide for breaking ice in Thunder Bay and Lake Superior and other points deemed advisable for the good of navigation, $40,000.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
This item is to provide
for ice-breaking in Thunder bay, lake Superior and other points. Thirty thousand dollars is the amount spent for breaking ice in Thunder bay for the purpose of keeping navigation open to as late a date as possible in order that the grain vessels may get down i to the harbours in the lakes below. The contract of -the Canadian Towing and Wrecking Company amounts to $30,000 for three years. There is a small amount of $500 that is _ paid on a contract with a tug owner, to keep open the navigable channel from different points on the north shore from the date when the regular passenger boats on this route cease running in the autumn'until the ice is sufficiently strong to enable horses to cross in safety. The people living on St. John island have to go to the mainland to their market, which, I think, it at Sault Ste. Marie. The only other item is one of $300 for keeping open the River Ste. Croix between St. Stephen, New Brunswick, vand Calais, Maine. A similar amount of $300 is paid by the Government of the United States. In addition, we watch very carefully every fall as to the necessity of ice-breaking in the Sault river for the purpose of getting the grain down at the very last moment. This year it was not necessary in that case, but every year we find it necessary to watch it.

As this item is in connection with the coastal service, I desire to bring to the attention of the minister, and of the other ministers who are present in the House, a report which appears in to-night's Toronto Globe, and in regard to which, I think, it would be only fair to give an assurance to the people living along the border of the province of Ontario. The item in the Globe is headed: " Plotted against Sarnia tunnel - San Francisco indictments against German officials-Scores of charges laid." The despatch is from San Francisco, dated February 11, and it states:

A total of 61 indictments were returned here to-day (by the federal grand jury in the alleged German bomb and shipping plot cases.
It gives the names of the Germans, and mentions that three hundred other individuals and firms were accused. Then it goes on to say that several of these men whose names are mentioned, have been indicted on a general charge of conspiring to set on foot a military expedition against Canada from within the borders of the United States. In view of the reports, published within the last day or two, that Germany proposes, on and after the first of March, to recommence her submarine warfare, I think the matter requires consideration. I am not in any sense desirous of being an alarmist, but it has struck me in this sense,_ and _ I think the Government should consider it, that if Germany's threat is carried out it would have the effect, perhaps, of stirring up German feeling in the States, and it would 'be well for the people of this country to have an assurance from the Government that everything possible is being done for the protection of our frontier I repeat that I do not in the least desire to be an alarmist, nor do I desire to raise questions which ought not to be raised at the present time. Nevertheless, one cannot help feeling, and one cannot shut his eyes to the fact that there is a grave situation as between the United States and Germany, and that in view of the number of German people in the United States and in Canada an exceedingly serious situation might arise. In these circumstances I think it would be well, if it is not asking too much of the Government at the present time, to have some assurance that all steps are being taken to safeguard the frontier.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: I am very glad to be able to give my hon. friend the assurance that every possible precaution is being taken to see that points along the frontier, which might be referred to as strategic points, where there is a danger of damage being done, are protected. There is' a secret service organized for that purpose, and every vigilance is being observed. It cannot be conceived that the United States would allow its frontier to be used as a base for attack upon Canada. Every possible precaution, I can assure my hon. friend, is being taken to prevent anything of the sort.

What gives colour to this thing is that one of the persons against whom proceedings are now being taken in San Francisco in connection with plots
against Canada is Francis Bopp, Consular General of Germany at Montreal for many years, who was a familiar figure in days gone by there, who frequently attended the openings of Parliament here, and who was thoroughly acquainted with everything connected with Parliament and the country.

I noticed in last year's Auditor General's Report that there was a certain sum of money paid to Sir Cecil Spring-Rice for ice patrols and the destruction of derelicts. I assume there is some international -arrangement between Canada and the United States in regard to this work. It would be interesting to the committee to know what arrangement has been made between the two countries, and if it is in existence at the present time, or whether it was simply an arrangement for one year.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: That amount was paid under an agreement come to at the International Convention for the Safety of Ships at Sea. My hon. friend will remember that three years ago a conference was held in London at which all the maritime nations wcto represented and at which the Deputy Minister of Marine and Fisheries was the representative of the Canadian Government. An agreement was come to in regard to the lifeboats that should be carried, the draught of ships and different precautions for the safety of ships and of persons travelling upon them. Among other questions considered was that of the removal of derelicts. Sometimes a derelict would be found floating around the Atlantic ocean outside of territorial waters and it would not be the special business of any one to remove it. An agreement was come to by which, as regards the North Atlantic ocean, the Government of the United States would undertake the work of removing derelicts.
What proportion of the cost are we liable for?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: There is a scale agreed upon under which each nation which uses these waters shall contribute its share. The amount we contribute is two per cent of the cost.
We are not carrying on any observations of our own with regard to icebergs and derelicts?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
No, it was felt by the
members of the convention that the best way would be to place the responsibility upon the shoulders of one of the parties to

the convention, and allow the
9 p.m. others to contribute to the cost. The amount which we pay as our share, two per cent,. I have always thought a very reasonable part of the c-os-t.
Who pays the other ninety-eight per cent?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: Great Britain pays twenty per cent of the whole, we pay two per cent, the United States twenty per cent, and France, I think, fifteen per cent. Other nations pay a share.

I notice by the press
that the Grand Trunk Pacific intend to operate a line of boats regularly between Prince Rupert and Alaska. I think they say that it is to be a weekly service, but I forget at what perio.ds the service is to be performed; at all events, it is a regular service. Will that necessitate any further expense along the route between these two points on account of the extra traffic for increased lighting?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: I do not think so. That coast is very well lighted. We have put in a very extensive system of lights in recent years. Three years ago I went up as far as Skagway and came down through the Alaskan -territory. Large and expensive steamers have been running on that route for a great many years. I would fancy that a great deal of the route traversed by those boats lies in American waters. It may be necessary that some- further lights are required in Canadian waters but at the present time I do not think that any very great expenditure would he required for that purpose.

Perhaps I can enlighten my hon. friend from South Renfrew (Mr. Graham), as I have to travel over that route while coming to this Parliament and going back home. As he will recall,
' Prince Rupert is just south of the Portland canal, which is the boundary line between Alaska and British, Columbia. Within a few hours from the time the boats leave Prince Rupert they are in American waters, and from there to the port in Alaska, to which they run, Skagway, the coast is lighted, as far as it is lighted, by the American Government. As far as the Canadian section of the route is concerned, I fancy there will be no extra expense.
Is it well lighted?

I tell the Americans that it is not lighted as well as our section

is. I think the section we are responsible for is lighted very much better; in fact, I always feel safer when I get within range of our own lights, although it is all fairly well lighted.
Lighthouse and coast service-repairs to Maritime road, $1,000.
Is that in Gaspe county? Mr. HAZEN: Yes .
The usual amount?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: Yes.
Could not a larger amount be voted for that road so that it might be made more permanent?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
No, I think we are voting all we can be expected to, It was put there originally as a road for our telegraph line, an aid to navigation. The whole country is now practically settled, and if there is need for $1,000 now, there was a greater necessity for a larger amount years ago. I was down on that coast last year, on my way to Anticosti, and it seemed that, looking . at it from the steamer, although I went ashore at Gaspe, the coast was remarkably well settled. There is no reason for voting any more. I doubt if there is any great necessity for this, but inasmuch as it is a help to the people there,
I do not like to strike it out of the Estimates.

It is much needed.
What my hon. friend the minister saw while looking from the ship were settlements at the mouths of the various little rivers, but some of the largest sections of the road are probably in the mountains bordering the river St. Lawrence. Originally the amount was voted for the maintenance of the telegraph line, it being a Government line.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: This is where the telegraph line connects with Anticosti, is it not?

Yes. I would advise my hon. friend, when he takes a jaunt down the river, to stop on the coast and see for himself in what state the road is. Several sections of the road have been repaired by the Provincial Government, but really, if a round sum, say something like $10,000, were spent, he could locate part of the road elsewhere, and then have a permanent road and stop paying this $1,000 yearly. I would be pleased to see my hon. friend on that coast, which is a very hospitable one, and perhaps if he saw the road he would change

his mind with regard to the item under [DOT]discussion.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: This item is'$300 less than it was last year, because one of the pilots has died.
Were these pilots retired in the natural way, or were they asked to retire?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
The arrangement is a very old one. The hon. gentlemen will recall that a good many years ago The Canada Shipping Act fixed the number of pilots at Quebec as not exceeding 125. It was felt by all the maritime interests at Quebec that it was not in the interest of the shipping of the port that there should be
t
so many pilots. An arrangement was come to, therefore, I think early in 1903 or 1904, by which these men were to retire at a certain age until the number got down to seventy-five, and on retirement	they
were to receive a pension of $600, of which	$300	was to be	paid
out of the pilot fund and $300 by Parliament. This arrangement, which was made by the Administration of which my hon. friend was a member, was made undoubtedly in the belief that it was in the interest of the shipping of the St. Lawrence ports. We are simply carrying out that arrangement.
Is it intended that this arrangement shall be extended to other parts of Canada?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: The arrangement was made at the time with regard only to the river St. Lawrence and the Quebec pilots. There are two sets of pilots, one at Quebec and one at, Montreal.

Why should we pension the Quebec pilots and not the pilots at Halifax, St. John, Canso, and other ports in Canada?
' Mr. HAZEN: The time to have fought out that question was when this arrangement was come to and confirmed by Parliament, which was some years before I became Minister of Marine and Fisheries.
IS there an Aet of Parliament authorizing the payment of these pensions? Does this mean that the pilots are permanent pensioners on the revenues of Canada for all time to come?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: During their lifetime.
Is this confined to the river St. Lawrence and only to a certain number of pilots on that river?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
Yes. I will read the information I have on the subject, but substantially my hon. friend has stated the case:
In connection with the Government allowance to supplement pension of certain Quebec pilots, it may be said:
Section 443 of the Canada Shipping Act fixes the number of Quebec pilots at not exceeding 125.
Section 434 declares that the existing rate of pilotage shall not be altered unless the net income of each member of the Quebec Pilots! Corporation acting and practising as a pilot has been less than $600 on an average for three consecutive years immediately preceding, in which case it shall be the duty of the Minister of Marine and Fisheries to submit to the Governor in Council for approval a by-law estab-

lishing such increased rates of pilotage as are deemed necessary to secure the pilots an annual income of not less than $600.	,
On the 20th of July, 1905, the Minister of Marine and Fisheries replaced the Harbour Commissioners of Quebec as the pilotage authority for the pilotage district of Quebec (4-5 Edward VII, chapter 34, section 2). At that date there were 118 pilots on the list.
The shipping interests in Quebec among others Wrote the department in 1904 complaining of the excessive number of licensed pilots. They said, " If the present large number of Quebec pilots is retained the pilotage rates will have to be increased so as to give each member of the corporation a stipend of $600 per season as provided by law. This will add considerable additional expense to the St. Lawrence route, which is already too expensive."
It was deemed advisable by the department to forestall any such demand for increased pilotage rates. Steps were therefore taken to reduce the number of pilots to a maximum of 75 and a minimum of 70, which was generally agreed would be sufficient for the service. To bring about this, it was necessary to make some provision for the pension of the pilots to be retired. The pilots' 'fund was only paying some $215 by way of pension at that time. The Pilots' Corporation agreed to bring their contribution up to $300 a year for the pensions of those pilots who would be compulsorily retired under the arrangement to reduce the number of licensed pilots to 70, provided the department contributed a like amount. This would make a payment of $600 a year to those pilots, which was the minimum rate of average earnings under section 434 of the Canada Shipping Act.
In a memorandum made by Commander Spain about the end of March, 1906, it is stated that the 'Government contribution of $300 a year to each Quebec pilot on retirement would continue until the number was reduced to 75.
An Order in Council was passed on the 5th of December, 1906, authorizing the payment by Government of a grant of $300 per annum as pension to all Quebec pilots on reaching the age limit of 65 years, and a similar pension to those under that age if retired on ground of physical incapacity. There is no mention of the fact that this arrangement is to apply only until the number of pilots is reduced to 75.
The contention of the pilots is supported by the correspondence which they have, and by the fact that the agreement come to was that future pilots who were pensioned would receive $300 from, the Government even when the number fell below seventy. The number of pilots now in active service is between seventy and seventy-five.
Mr.. SINCLAIR: Who has control of the appointments of these pilots, so that they may not increase in number indefinitely?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
The pilots licenses are issued to-day by our department. We have an official in charge. This is in compliance with the recommendation made by the Pilotage Commission, and so far as I can find out, the conditions, which for-

merly were not satisfactory, are infinitely more satisfactory now. The number , of pilots will not be allowed to increase unless the shipping of the country increases tremendously, far more than is expected. It is a matter of history in the department, and I am giving the facts as they are given to me. According to that statement of facts, the Government of the day came to the conclusion-I will not say unfairly or unwisely-that the only way to get the number of pilots down was to supplement by $300 a year the pension the pilots received from, the Pension Fund.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
The matter has been taken up and taken up very seriously, and great reforms have been made. We appointed a commission made up of a representative of the Shipping Federation of Canada, and representatives of other shipping interests. The commission went into the matter with the greatest possible care. As a result of its inquiry, the commission made recommendations, and every one of those recommendations has been carried into effect. In consequence of this, I understand, pilotage on the St. Lawrence is in a condition more satisfactory to the shipping interests and to all others affected by this business than it has ever been before. My hon. friend (Mr. Sinclair) raises the question of the necessity of compulsory pilotage. That question has been discussed in practically every part of the world. You can find the greatest divergence among shipping people on this subject. The question is raised why the vessel that does not take a pilot should be required to pay pilotage dues. Well, the argument that has prevailed practically everywhere is this. It is absolutely 'necessary, for the safety of shipping, to have an, efficient corps of pilots. With the great commerce on the river St. Lawrence, and in view of the character of the navigation from the Gulf to Quebec and from Quebec to Montreal, practically through a channel which, though-lighted, requires local knowledge to understand the lights, I do not see how any one can argue that you could get along without an efficient corps of pilots. Very well, how are you going to maintain them? There are some captains who would take the risk and pilot their own vessels. But if you allow' these captains who have local knowledge to pilot themselves and not pay towards the pilotage fund, the earnings oE pilots will be reduced, and so you will not be able to maintain a corps of trained, intelligent, efficient men to act as pilots. As a result,
you will have disasters to the sbijos coming into the port. That is the argument that has, appealed to the shipping people in most places.
My hon. friend condemns the system on the St. Lawrence in another respect. He says that there should not be one pilotage district from Montreal to Quebec and another from Quebec to the sea. I do not think he will get the owners of the large liners that run to Montreal to agree with him, the men to whom-as they have large sums of money invested-it is of the utmost importance to have efficient pilots. The distance from Father Point, where the pilot is usually taken on, to Montreal is 350 miles. A pilot on a boat travelling at a rate of fifteen miles an hour would have to be at his post about twenty-three hours ,in bringing the vessel from Father point to Montreal. No pilot could stand on the bridge of a ship and direct its movements for twenty-three hours; he would probably sleep at his post and endanger the safety of the vessel. My hon. friend will find it to be the general opinion of those who have large sums of money invested in the liners which pass between Quebec and Montreal that it is necessary to have two pilots in order to bring the vessel from Father Point to Montreal. This route will be much easier of navigation when the work which is now being carried on is finished. I do not say that it is very dangerous, but in thick weather great care must be -taken in guiding the ship through the Traverse and the ranges of lights along that route. The pilot who brings a vessel from Father point to Montreal must be constantly on the alert. The route from Quebec to Montreal is practically a lane running in different directions and full of sharp curves; after bringing a vessel from Father point to Quebec, the pilot would not be in physical condition immediately to take that vessel from Quebec to Montreal. Considering the fact that the navigation between Quebec and Montreal is as I have described, one would think that accidents along that route would be numerous; but it is a curious fact that that route has been practically free from accidents while accidents happen when there is plenty of sea room on either side, due, I suppose, to some error in judgment. I can assure the hon. member for Guysborough that when I came to the department this matter was discussed from every standpoint; a commission was appointed representing the different interests concerned, and improved

conditions have resulted, practically no complaint now being made by the shipping interests. No doubt some captains could guide their own vessels with safety, and it may be a little hardship on them to pay pilotage; but that is a condition of affairs that occurs almost everywhere. Besides, the time may come when those men, under circumstances of bad weather, may be glad to get a pilot to bring them safely into port. Under any system, I care not what it may be, there is generally something objectionable to some one. On the whole, however, I think this system is working splendidly. The pilots are under the direction of a superintendent directly responsible to the Department of Marine and ^Fisheries, and the system 'has given more general satisfaction and is attended with less risk and fewer accidents than has been the case for many years past.

My hon. friend has given every possible argument which could be advanced by the pilots, but he has not dealt with the interests of the shippers. I assure my hon. friend that there. is no such system as this in any. of the great ports of Europe. There is no compulsory pilotage in the port of New York, which is the destination of many more ships than pass up the river St. Lawrence.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: The conditions there are very different.

Compulsory pilotage is justifiable only when there is a scarcity of pilots; when you cannot find men who will devote themselves to the business of piloting ships, and who will be always on hand when ships arrive. The real origin of compulsory pilotage was the lack of men who were willing to take the responsibility of waiting for the vessels as they came in, the result being that in many cases vessels were unable to obtain pilots when they wanted them. But in the river St. Lawrence, where large numbers of men are competing for the pilotage business, there is not the slightest need for any system of compulsory' pilotage. The system exists only for the purpose of creating revenue for the pilots; if they did not have1 political influence' and the control of three or four hundred votes no such system would exist in Canada to-day. This system has been established and maintained in the river St. Lawrence through the political influence of the pilots; I am not saying that one party is more to blame than the other, but 
we all know that this is a fact. We may assume that every ship travelling on the St. Lawrence and arriving at the port of Montreal is insured.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: The insurance rates would go up very considerably if no pilots were *available there.

In cases where the insurance companies provide that if the vessel goes ashore or any accident happens, the insurance shall not be paid, the owners will take good care to get a pilot. Under the present system of wireless telegraphy, it is the easiest thing in the world for the captain of a vessel approaching the coast to arrange for his pilot to meet him at a certain point. The agent of the owner at. Montreal or Quebec can get in touch with a responsible pilot and arrange that the-pilot shall meet the vessel at Father Point, or wherever he may be required. That is the way it is done in New York, Liverpool and London; why should it not be done that way on the river St. Lawrence?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: How does the approach by water to the city of New York compare with the approach to the city of Montreal?

I am aware that there is a difference, but that is no reason why the ship owner should not be allowed to employ his own pilot. He will find his pilot just as he finds every other man whom he wants in his service; it is quite unnecessary for the' public to find a pilot for him or to compel him to take a pilot if ,he does not want one. If he is a competent captain and can take the ship to port himself, he may not need a pilot; if he does need one, he gets the man he wants. That is the business way of doing this thing, and when the Dominion of Canada gets a little older, that is the way it will be done. It would be a credit to the port of Montreal and it would make trade cheaper and more satisfactory in every way if this most intolerable system were discontinued and the people allowed to do their own business and employ their own pilots.

Have the pilots in my hon. friend's constituency made request for a provision similar to that which applies to the Quebec pilots? I fear for my hon. friend, and somewhat for myself as well- that if this discussion comes before the pilots pf the Maritime Provinces, we shall hear something about it in the future.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: We have had this discussion year after year.

When the pilots of the Maritime Provinces read this discussion, * they may desire to obtain the same provision for themselves. I would think that the provisions which apply to the pilots in Quebec should apply also to pilots in other parts of the Dominion. How long have these men to be in the business before they become licensed pilots?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
' The Quebec pilots are practically born and brought up in the service. They enter as apprentices, serve a certain length of time on river vessels, and a certain length of time on deep sea vessels. They usually start as boys; they can not become pilots after they are 30 years of age.
Mr. H. BOULAY (Rimouski). (Translation.) Mr. Chairman, I should not allow to go unanswered the references to the pilots which have just been made by the hon. member for Guysborough. The hon. gentleman is greatly mistaken when he proclaims in this House and for the information of the country at large, that our pilots are of no use. My whole life was *spent on the shores of the >St. Lawrence. Every year shipwrecks have occurred, and that very often when the ships were under the guidance of very capable pilots, who had made the trip, practically two or three times a month. Nevertheless shipwrecks will happen. And of course, if ships of the large size of those which are at present doing the service between the old country and Canada, were left under the sole guidance of the captain, you may be sure that accidents would be not only as numerous, but would increase three-fold and four-fold.
Possibly the hon. gentleman never ascended the St. Lawrence in a ship, otherwise he would have noticed the numerous breakers which the pilots have to avoid before getting to port.
I hope the views expressed by the hon. gentleman in regard to the usefulness of pilots will not prevail.
Could the minister give us any information as to the comparative rates of insurance on the Canadian and American routes?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
That subject is dealt with by the Department of Trade and Commerce. Of course, the comparison is slightly against the St. Lawrence route, as the insurance companies regard it as an extra hazard when a vessel has to enter a river.
Representations are being constantly made by the shipping men to the Government on the subject, and, as a matter of fact, there has been a very great lowering of the St. Lawrence rates owing to the increased safety of that route on account of the improved aids to navigation. But the insurance rates are not yet as low as the New York rates.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works
speechtext:
The difference is about sixpence a quarter.
Telephones in connection with aids to navigation, $5,000.	.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
I would move that that item be reduced to $500. It has been inseited in the Estimates year after year at $5,000, but I do. not know why. For the year 1914-15 we spent under it $8.50, and up to the 31st of December this year $1.50.
Item, as amended, agreed to,
New Vessel to replace the Maisonneuve, $2,500.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
This vessel has been out of commission for the past three years. She was condemned as absolutely unfit for service, and we have sold her at about the price she would bring for junk. We were given this vote last year, but in consequence of conditions connected with the war we have been trying to make expenses as light as possible, and so we chartered the Maggie May, which did the lighthouse work on the Ottawa river during the last year.
Allowance to harbour master at Amherst-burg for supervision of lights and buoys on St. Clair river, the Detroit river, and lake Brie, $400.
What lights does he take care of?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
We have no agency in that district, and this official brings in the buoys in the fall and puts them out in the spring. The buoys are, of course, very valuable, and must be taken in before the ice comes, and we have found this to be the most economical way of dealing with them.
Repairing C. G. S. Montmagny, $70,000.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
This vessel was sunk in
collision. We advertised for tenders for raising her, and the contract was awarded to the lowest tenderer, the Levis Wrecking Company, at $27,977. The contractors have to raise the boat and deliver it at the wharf at Levis. Then it will cost $70,000 to put the vessel in proper condition for service. The vessel was built in Sorel and cost

$275,000, so that it is well worth while spending this $70,000, as she will then be in as good condition as a new vessel.
Will the repairs be made in the Government shipyard?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: We have not decided that yet.
If not, I presume public tenders will be called for.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: Yes, if the work is of such a character that a specification on which to call for tenders can be made by the engineer.	*
She was sunk at the Isle d'Orleans?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
Yes.
%
Were any lives lost?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: Yes, a number.

Were claims made by
the dependents of those lost?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
An inquiry was conducted by Captain Demers, whose report was a severe arraignment of the officers of the boat. One man who lost his life in the wreck was reported to have acted like a hero, and we made provision for his family.
Marine hospitals, including: grants to institutions assisting sailors, $75,000.
What does that include?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
This is for the Marine Hospital service. It is difficult to determine from year to year the amount required to cover the expenditure for this service. It is necessary to vote a sum which frequently is in excess of the amount required. In 1914-15 we spent $65,477, and . up to the 31st December, this year, we had spent $48,008. It is expected that the amount asked for will be more than enough to cover the expenditure during the coming year unless something unforeseen happens.
Air. GRAHAM,: How many institutions are there?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
There used to be one in almost every shipping port, but they have been nearly all abolished. A marine hospital is not maintained at any port or in any city where there is a public hospital. There are only four marine hospitals in existence at the present time. The system which prevails is that, in a city where there is a public hospital, we have an arrangement by which the hospital authorities

take care of the sick sailors at so much per day. We pay $1.50 per day at the present time, and it costs the country very much less than under the old system, while the sailors really?, get better attention than formerly.

This amount includes, I understand, the amounts paid to doctors who attend sick seamen outside of the hospitals. There are certain ports where there are no hospitals, and it is a unique condition-at least I regard it as such-that a seaman going from- one port to another in the same province does not get the benefit of the sick mariners' fund. If a seaman, for instance, should leave the province of Nova Scotia and go to the Magdalen islands, a distance of 20 or 25 miles, he is entitled to benefit under that fund; but, if he leaves any port of the province and goes to another port in the province, he does not get the benefit. I would like to know from the minister the reason foT that.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: No sick seamen's dues are collected from vessels that go from one port in the province to another port in the same province. . If a vessel goes from one port in a province to another port in another province, the vessel pays the dues. I suppose the reason why the benefit of the fund does not apply to vessels going from one port in a province to another port in the same province is that it was thought they would be near their homes, and that therefore it would be unfair to collect dues from them.

The mariners
themselves do not regard it as an advantage not to pay the dues. They regard it as a privilege to pay them. It is an extraordinary condition of things that a seaman leaving, we will say, a port in the province of Nova Scotia and perhaps going 300 or 400 miles away from home, does not get the benefit of the fund, whereas if he just crosses the straits, or to a neighbouring province, he does get the benefit. The seamen are anxious to have the privilege of paying their dues. The fee is a small one, according to tonnage, I think, but it gives the sailors a very great privilege. This is not the first time I have' brought the matter to the attention of the minister; in fact, I brought it to the attention of the late Government, and to the attention of the minister last year. I would like to see some regulation by which if this benefit is to obtain at all, it would be neces-

sary for the mariner to go outside of his province to get it.
Mr. PARI)Eli; Do these grants apply to sailors on inland waters?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: No, the dues are paid only by sailors of salt water ships.
Suppose a doctor should report that a seaman is being attended to, and the ship should go away without his being paid, is the Government responsible for the payment.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: It is up to the Marine Department.
What is the condition of this fund at the present time?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: The receipts from the fund are larger than the expenditure. In 1914 the receipts were $72,602.43, and the expenditures $65,397.85.
Can the minister tell us what the total surpluses have been since the introduction of the fund.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: I car.ot tell that, but I have the receipts and expenditures since 1901. In 1904 the receipts were $61,000 and the expenditure $50,000; in 1911 the receipts were $67,000 and the expenditure- $54,779; and in 1913, the receipts were $70,000 and the expenditures $54,000. There must- be a considerable sum to the credit of the fund.

I would like to inform the minister that his officers are very strict in the administration of this fund. If they were as careful in regard to other matters connected with the Government as they are with regard to this fund, we would not have such big deficits. I am constantly receiving, complaints from sailors who have been treated in the most technical way by officers of the department in connection with the administration of this fund. There ought to be some compassionate allowance, if no other. Let me give the minister one case. A sailor, by the name of Captain Angus Macdonald became ill on the coast of Cape Breton while navigating his ship and he was sent to the hospital in North Sydney. His family who live in my county were very anxious about him, and before he was altogether fit to be removed, he was taken out of the hospital by his family who were anxious to get him home.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: Against the advice of the hospital authorities?
He became so ill that he was unable to complete the journey home, and he was put in a boarding house.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: I know all about it.
I want to make my case first.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: It is unnecessary to make your case, because we have paid the amount. It was before me this morning for the first time, and I decided that it was a fair and proper thing that the bills should be paid.

I am very glad to hear that. But your officers rejected that claim, and this widow had to go without her money for many months, to consult lawyers and get them to write affidavits and make statements in order to have her claim settled. That should not be the case. When legitimate claims of this kind come before you, although you may not be technically liable, they should be paid. This widow should not have been put to all the annoyance and trouble that she was put to.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: If my hon. friend argued the matter much longer I would be almost afraid that I had made a mistake in ordering these bills paid. I am not disposed to find fault with my officials for what they did. The matter was brought to my attention for the first time this morning, and I thought I was leaning to the side of generosity in doing what I did. This man was in hospital, he was being treated there, he left the hospital contrary to the advice of those who were responsible for him, when he was not in a condition of health to go. He went away to another town and took ill there, and a doctor and nurse were called in. Under these circumstances, if they were dealing with it as a matter of absolutely strict justice, I would not be disposed to say that our officials were wrong. It is the business of the officials of the department to deal with things from the correct, legal standpoint, and in the interests of the treasury. The minister feels that he has a good deal more liberty than his officials, and, after weighing the whole case, I thought it was safer to err on the side of generosity rather than be too strict. So this morning, after going over the case with the official who has charge of that work and the deputy minister, I gave directions that these bills should be paid.
Is the minister disposed to remove that difficulty that I have referred to?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: Does my hon. friend think that the men who are interested as owners of vessels in his part of Nova Scotia would prefer to have the advantages of this Act on condition that they pay to the fund just as others do if they are travelling from port to port in their own province?

That is my opinion. I took the trouble to get the opinions of those people that I happened to meet, and I am disposed to think that they are very anxious to have that right. It would save them a good deal of trouble. It is a great encouragement for the men who go aboard a ship to know that they are protected in respect to this matter. I know that^ sailors prefer to go on a vessel that is plying from one province to another rather than a vessel plying between ports of the same province. A man may become ill, and he knows that when he falls into the hands of a medical man he will be well looked after. I would like to see that disability removed for the benefit of mariners.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
That is an old provision of the Act. I have been intending to bring the amendments to the Canada
10 p.m. Shipping Act, which I had prepared a couple of years ago, before Parliament, but last year it was not thought desirable that there should be any more legislation than could possibly be avoided, except legislation in connection with the war, and the position seems to be the same this year. I will give what consideration I can to it, and endeavour to ascertain what the reasons were at the time of the passage of the Bill for the enactment of this provision. If I feel that it imposes any undue hardship upon the shipping interests I shall feel disposed to favour a change.

A petition was presented to the department by the lighthouse keepers asking for the establishment of a retiring fund. Has the minister any project in his mind looking to the granting of the prayer of this petition? Has he any scheme of his own for the establishment of a retiring fund for lighthouse keepers?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
There was a superannuation existing for civil servants, which Parliament repealed a few years ago. Those who enter the service now, with a few exceptions, such as the judges, have no superan-

nuation secured to them, and it is a little difficult to see why, that being the case, lighthouse keepers should be placed upon a different plane from other employees of the Government, and those engaged in other pursuits, for instance, engineers and conductors upon the railways. It may be that lighthouse keepers can make some arrangement amongst themselves, as the railway men do. I do not see how this Government, in view of the position that Parliament took in repealing the superannuation system, could inaugurate a system for the lighthouse keepers alone.
Was that the answer given to the lighthouse keepers when their petition was presented? They want to know if you are going to allow them a retiring fund.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
I do not remember what the correspondence was. I will look it up tomorrow. If they want to form a fund the officers of my department will give them all the assistance and advice they can.
Mr. GAtJVEEAU: Will there be any assistance from the Government if they undertake to establish a fund for themselves? Will the Government be prepared to give them a sum of money with which to start their retiring, or pension, fund?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: I am not prepared to say that at present. There are difficulties in the way. You are treating one class differently from another. If we are to have any system of retiring allowances, or Government assistance, it should be made to apply pretty generally to all classes of employees.
They have such a system on the Intercolonial railway.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: Do the Government give any assistance?,
Yes.
The Government give a certain amount, just as the railway companies give a certain amount to their employees.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: Something might be done on that line.
So that we can understand that there is hope that they will have some relief from the Government?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
We shall be very glad to look into the matter. [DOT]
Progress reported.

On the motion of Mr. Rogers the House adjourned at 10.08 p.m.
Monday, February 14, 1916.
